fields.v: Pinto, G., de Freitas, E. R. S., Ribeiro, D. M. (2026). Is This Code Mine? Student Ownership When AI Agents Write the Spec and the Code. arXiv:2611.21501v1 [cs.SE], 16 Nov 2026
Preprint — arXiv:2611.21501v1 [cs.SE], 16 Nov 2026; IEEE conference format, no published venue stated
Federal University of Para (UFPA), Brazil (Pinto, de Freitas); CESAR School, Recife, Brazil (Ribeiro)

Evaluates — observational educational study: mining of the 18 student repositories built with AI coding agents under SDD, their recorded prompts, and a survey of 33 students on psychological ownership (RQ1-RQ5)

Course SDD workflow (spec -> plan -> tasks presented in class; no named framework or version), with assignment conventions: dated specs in SPEC/ (YYYY-MM-DD-<part>.md) committed before code, commit trailers Agent: and Spec:, recorded session exports. One team used OpenSpec (version Not stated). Spec Kit and Kiro cited as supporting tools

Dated specification per part of the system stating what and why, verifiable acceptance criteria and out-of-scope; new dated file to replace a spec on change of direction; prompts/sessoes/ session exports; commit trailers Agent: and Spec:. Plan and tasks presented in class but not required as files
Specification -> plan -> tasks -> agent implements one task at a time against the specification (as presented); assignment only enforced spec-before-code
Not prescribed by the assignment beyond students being expected to specify, direct, review and test; individual oral defence in later project; recommended: student draft of each spec, oral checks
Specification format and spec-first convention (plus whatever students did); full workflow not verified
Not stated in Boeckeler's terms; authors: 'In SDD, the specification is the artifact the human owns, and the code is its consequence' (spec-first in the assignment)
New project (greenfield): each pair had to build and publish a non-trivial application of their choice with a target of at least 100,000 lines of code in one week (only 3 of 18 reached the target)
18 projects, 780,614 SLOC total (median 11,115; min 753, max 201,848); 1,051 commits (795 by agent); 277 specifications (median 544 words); only 3 projects reached 100k, all via unused generated code
Web applications (booking and scheduling, clinics, salons, games, etc.); TypeScript (9), Python (7), Java/Angular (1), JavaScript (1)

36 students in 18 pairs (33 surveyed) of an elective course in Latin America (Brazil); 82% in 7th-8th semester; 52% programming 3-5 years; 64% worked in software development (mostly interns); 70% use AI daily but only 21% had let an agent work autonomously; 39% had never written a spec before
None measured objectively; self-reported hours dedicated (median 8 h, Q1 5, Q3 14); students mentioned subscription and token costs qualitatively

Public production URL listed in the README (17/18; whether it works is not checked); automated tests present (14 projects, 3,896 test cases, not required; 4 run them in CI); functional correctness not measured
Duplicated/unreachable code and filler (requirement gaming audit): e.g. DeliveryFast 99.5%, Trim 97%, UmbraTrail 29% of lines unused generated code

Self-reported: hours dedicated (median 8), share of generated code read before committing (median 30%); share of ideas (median 50%) and code (median 20%) attributed to self; prompts per session (741 prompts, median 15 words)

SDD adherence (spec first 53-90%, sessions recorded, trailers 69% median); spec authorship (by agent 69%), structure (acceptance criteria 86%, what/why 91%, out of scope 85%), traceability (referenced 71%, with code 14%, revised 12%, lines traced 39%); perceived ownership of code (mean 3.29), of spec/app (3.27), knowledge of code (2.71); requirement gaming cases

Automatic: scripts over cloned git histories (trailers, file names, regex, cloc 1.98), session parsers (87/109 sessions parsed), GitHub activity API for force pushes; duplicate/unreachable code heuristics. Manual: gaming candidates inspected by one author and reviewed by a second; open answers coded by one author, reviewed by a second. Survey: Google Forms, 28 questions, 38 Likert items (Cronbach alpha), Wilcoxon and Spearman (no correction, exploratory)

- Course SDD conventions + agents chosen freely (Claude Code 10 projects, Codex 5, Antigravity/Gemini 5, GitHub Copilot 3, also OpenCode, DeepSeek, ChatGPT; 7 teams used more than one) + models Not stated per project (trailer example claude-code/claude-sonnet-5-5): criterion: assignment rules and SDD conventions; no per-agent breakdown. Results: specs mostly agent-written (69%), only 39% of lines traced to a spec, 14% of specs added with code; 3 teams reached 100k lines only with unused generated code, 1 team backdated specs by rewriting history. Quality verdict: does not work (SDD conventions followed unevenly; specs did not keep students in control). Cost verdict: not measured

N/A: no configurations compared; observational, 18 teams with free choice of domain, stack and tools; within-pair comparison of member with more vs fewer commits (14 pairs); no repetitions; no rules for human intervention beyond assignment conventions

N/A (no configuration comparison). Within pairs, member with more commits reports higher code ownership (median 3.64 vs 2.71, p = 0.046) but not higher knowledge (p = 0.37). Ideas vs code self-attribution differ (p < 0.001). Mined team measures do not correlate with ownership
N/A

Trailer-based attribution gives lower bounds; spec-first not computable for 3 projects; heading-based structure detection; self-reported ownership; 22 sessions unparsable; grading may shape declarations, social desirability; gaming heuristics catch only templated filler; one course, one university, 18 teams; RQ4 exploratory. Recommendations: scope-based targets, student-written spec drafts, enforce process with tooling/CI and AGENTS.md, mid-assignment requirement change, oral checks. Future: next course offering, semester project follow-up
